object.title: Gaussian moat
object.statement:
Let $\mathbb{Z}[i]=\{a+bi : a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ be the ring of Gaussian
integers, with norm
$N(a+bi)=a^{2}+b^{2}$ and Euclidean absolute value $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$.
Call $\pi\in\mathbb{Z}[i]$ a Gaussian prime if $\pi$ is a nonzero non-unit whose
only divisors in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ are units and unit multiples of $\pi$;
equivalently, $\pi$ is a Gaussian prime exactly when $N(\pi)$ is a rational
prime, or $\pi=u p$ with $u\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}$ and $p$ a rational prime with
$p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

Then there is no infinite sequence $\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\pi_{3},\dots$ of pairwise
distinct Gaussian primes such that

$$
\sup_{n\ge 1}\,\bigl|\pi_{n+1}-\pi_{n}\bigr|<\infty .
$$

Equivalently, for each real $k>0$ let $G_{k}$ be the graph whose vertex set is
the set of Gaussian primes and in which two distinct Gaussian primes
$\pi,\pi'$ are joined by an edge when $|\pi-\pi'|\le
k$; then every connected component of $G_{k}$ is finite. In particular, for
every $k>0$ the component of $G_{k}$ containing the Gaussian prime
$1+i$ is finite, so that only finitely many Gaussian primes can be reached from the origin by steps of length at most $k$
through Gaussian primes.
object.source_name: Wikipedia
object.references: 1. Wikipedia, [Gaussian moat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_moat), the article this problem comes from.

object.title: Conjecture on expressible elements in cyclic groups
object.statement:
Let $A$ be a cyclic group of order $m$. For $\boldsymbol{\pi}=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_m)\in(\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z})^m$ with $\pi_1\ge\cdots\ge\pi_m$, an element $x\in A$ is **$\boldsymbol{\pi}$-expressible** if, for some ordering $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ of the elements of $A$, one has

$$
x=g_1^{\pi_1}\cdots g_m^{\pi_m}.
$$

Let $\boldsymbol{\pi}'$ be obtained by subtracting $\pi_m$ from every part of $\boldsymbol{\pi}$, so that its last part is $0$. **Cyclic-group expressibility conjecture.** Every element of $A$ is $\boldsymbol{\pi}$-expressible unless either

1. $\boldsymbol{\pi}'=(m-r,r,0,\ldots,0)$ for some $r$, or
2. there exists an integer $p>1$ dividing every part of $\boldsymbol{\pi}'$ and also dividing $m$.

This conjecture gives a proposed classification of when all elements of a cyclic group occur as products determined by an exponent vector; the paper presents it as being supported by numerical evidence, while the stated exceptional cases are not asserted to be exhaustive in the source beyond this conjectural claim.
object.source_name: John R. Britnell and Mark Wildon, “On types and classes of commuting matrices over finite fields”, arXiv:1001.0811 (2010).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0811

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of January 2010).

object.title: Only integer-slope ceiling solutions for nested recursions
object.statement:
Let $r$ and $q$ be the parameters in the general nested recursion, and let $\left\lceil\frac{rn}{q}\right\rceil$ denote the corresponding ceiling function. **Integer-slope conjecture.** If $\left\lceil\frac{rn}{q}\right\rceil$ is the solution generated by a recursion of the form of the general recurrence, then $r=1$.

The conjecture is based on computer verification ruling out several examples with $r>1$, together with partial searches for another case; larger denominators were not checked because of computational cost. No proof or definitive disproof is given, so the conjecture remains open.
object.source_name: Abraham Isgur, Vitaly Kuznetsov and Stephen M. Tanny, “Nested recursions with ceiling function solutions”, arXiv:1204.6714 (2012).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.6714

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of April 2012).

object.title: The primitive-divisor conjecture for the sequence $2^d-3$
object.statement: For each positive integer $i$, consider the integer $2^i-3$. A **primitive prime divisor** of $2^d-3$ is a prime divisor that divides none of the earlier terms $2^i-3$ with $i<d$. **Primitive-divisor conjecture.** For every $d\ge 8$, there is a primitive prime divisor of $2^d-3$; equivalently, after checking the cases $d<8$, the Zsigmondy set of the sequence $(2^i-3)$ is exactly $\{1,2,7\}$. This conjecture is used only for a short conjectural proof of the nonexistence of the relevant subgroup; the paper also gives a complete longer proof, so the surrounding group-theoretic conclusion is established independently.
object.source_name: Karimah Sweet, Li Li, Eddie Cheng, László Lipták and Daniel E. Steffy, “A complete classification of which (n,k)-star graphs are Cayley graphs”, arXiv:1703.06111 (2017).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06111

Status: **open** according to the source (as of March 2017). “There is a conjecture that every finite connected Cayley graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle; for related work, see .”

object.title: The rank conjecture for the period matrix of linear algebraic cycles
object.statement:
Let $n$ be even, let $d_1,cldots,d_{\frac{n}{2}+1}$ be the cardinalities of subsets $B_1,B_2,c3,B_{\frac{n}{2}+1}$ of the set of complex roots of $zeta^d+1=0$, and let ${sf p}_i$ be defined by

$$
{sf p}_i:=prod_{k=0}^{\frac{n}{2}}sum_{zeta\text{ in }B_{k+1}}zeta^{i_{2k}+1}
$$

for $i$ in the specified index set, with ${sf p}_i=0$ otherwise. **Rank conjecture.** The matrix formed by the entries ${sf p}_{i+j}$ has rank

$$
{\operatorname{rank}([{sf p}_{i+j}])}={sf C}_{d_1,d_2,ldots,d_{\frac{n}{2}+1},d-d_1,d-d_2,ldots,d-d_{\frac{n}{2}+1}}.
$$

Here the number on the right is the quantity defined in the cited formula. This elementary linear-algebraic assertion is used in the proof of the paper's main theorem; the authors state that, apart from the first case, they do not know how to solve it in general and use computer calculations.
object.source_name: Hossein Movasati and Roberto Villaflor Loyola, “Periods of linear algebraic cycles”, arXiv:1705.00084 (2019).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.00084

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of May 2017).

object.title: Finite-monodromy classification for the families with p=2
object.statement:
Let $p=2$, and let ${\mathcal F}_d$ denote the family considered in the paper. The preceding corollaries establish finite monodromy when $d=2^a+1$ for some $a\geq 1$, and when $d=(2^a+1)/(2^b+1)$ with $a>b\geq 1$ and $a=bc$ for an odd integer $c$. **Finite-monodromy classification conjecture.** The family ${\mathcal F}_d$ has finite monodromy if and only if $d$ has one of these forms:

$$
d=2^a+1\quad\text{for some }a\geq 1,
$$

or

$$
d=\frac{2^a+1}{2^b+1}\quad\text{for some }b\geq 1\text{ and }a=bc\text{ with odd }c\geq 3.
$$

The conjecture asserts that the two families of examples supplied by the preceding corollaries exhaust all finite-monodromy cases when $p=2$; the source notes that this has been checked computationally for $d$ up to $10000$.
object.source_name: Antonio Rojas-Leon, “Finite monodromy of some families of exponential sums”, arXiv:1711.01584 (2018).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.01584

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of November 2017).

object.title: Conjecture on primitive weird numbers with arbitrarily many distinct prime factors
object.statement: Let $k\geq 3$ be an integer. **Conjecture.** There exists a primitive weird number having at least $k$ distinct prime factors. This would show that primitive weird numbers occur with arbitrarily many distinct prime factors; the source motivates the claim by the existence of weird numbers with six distinct prime factors, but gives no resolution.
object.source_name: Gianluca Amato, Maximilian F. Hasler, Giuseppe Melfi and Maurizio Parton, “Primitive weird numbers having more than three distinct prime factors”, arXiv:1803.00324 (2018).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.00324

Status: **open** according to the source (as of March 2018). “Another open question is the existence of odd weird numbers.”

object.title: Balletti–Kasprzyk conjecture on maximal-volume lattice polytopes with prescribed interior points
object.statement:
Let $d \ge 3$ and $k \ge 1$. Define the Sylvester sequence by

$$
s_1=2,\qquad s_i=1+s_1\cdots s_{i-1}\quad (i\ge 2),
$$

and let

$$
S_{d,k}:=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(o,s_1e_1,\ldots,s_{d-1}e_{d-1},(k+1)(s_d-1)e_d\bigr).
$$

Let $\mathcal{P}^d(k)$ be the family of all $d$-dimensional lattice polytopes with $k$ interior lattice points. **Balletti–Kasprzyk conjecture.** The simplex $S_{d,k}$ is a volume maximizer in $\mathcal{P}^d(k)$. Furthermore, with the exception of the case $d=3$, $k=1$, the volume maximizer in $\mathcal{P}^d(k)$ is unique up to unimodular transformations.

The simplex was introduced by Zaks, Perles and Wills and has $k$ interior lattice points. The conjecture was verified by complete enumeration for $d=3$, $k=1$ and $d=3$, $k=2$; its general case remains open.
object.source_name: Gennadiy Averkov, “Local optimality of Zaks-Perles-Wills simplices”, arXiv:1803.04852 (2018).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04852

Status: **solved** according to the source (as of March 2018). “Conjecture was verified by complete enumeration of $\cP^d(k)$ in the cases $d=3,\,k=1$ and $d=3,\, k=2$ in and , respectively.”

object.title: Firoozbakht's conjecture on successive prime roots
object.statement:
Let $p_n$ denote the $n$th prime, and let $n\geq1$. **Firoozbakht's conjecture.**

$$
(p_{n+1})^{1/(n+1)}\leq(p_n)^{1/n},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad {\ln p_{n+1}\over n+1}\leq{\ln p_n\over n}.
$$

This conjecture asserts a strong monotonicity property for the distribution of the primes. It has been verified computationally for all primes below substantial bounds, but no general proof is known.
object.source_name: Matt Visser, “Verifying the Firoozbakht, Nicholson, and Farhadian conjectures up to the 81st maximal prime gap”, arXiv:1904.00499 (2019).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00499

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of April 2019).

object.title: The generalised regularity classification for matrix semigroups over semirings
object.statement:
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be the semiring under consideration, and let $M_n(\mathfrak{L})$, $UT_n(\mathfrak{L})$, and $U_n(\mathfrak{L})$ denote the corresponding matrix semigroups. The table records their generalised regularity properties according to $n$: 

$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
 & n=1 & n=2 & n=3 & n\geq 4\\
\hline
M_n(\mathfrak{L}) & \text{Regular} & \text{Regular} & \text{Fountain (?) } & \text{Not Fountain}\\
UT_n(\mathfrak{L}) & \text{Regular} & \text{Abundant} & \text{Fountain (?) } & \text{Not Fountain}\\
U_n(\mathfrak{L}) & \text{Regular (group)} & \text{Regular (band)} & \text{Fountain} & \text{Fountain}
\end{array}
$$

**Generalised regularity classification.** The displayed classification summarises the generalised regularity properties of $M_n(\mathfrak{L})$, $UT_n(\mathfrak{L})$, and $U_n(\mathfrak{L})$ in the indicated cases.

The question marks in the $n=3$ entries indicate that those classifications are tentative rather than established assertions. Since the source presents this as a summary with unresolved entries, the precise status of the tentative cases should be checked against the paper's surrounding discussion.

object.title: Conjecture on uniqueness of rational maps from a numerator of a 3-cycle
object.statement:
Let $A(m,n)$ and $B(m,n)$ be the integer forms parametrizing rational $3$-cycles of maps $f_c(x)=x^2+c$, and let $(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ satisfy $mn(m+n)\neq0$ and $\gcd(m,n)=1$. **Numerator-uniqueness conjecture.** If $A(m,n)=k$, then $c=-A(m,n)/B(m,n)$ is the only rational number with numerator $k$ for which $f_c$ has a rational $3$-cycle. Equivalently, for $k\in\mathbb{N}$, the equation

$$
A(m,n)=m^6+2m^5n+4m^4n^2+8m^3n^3+9m^2n^4+4mn^5+n^6=k
$$

has either $0$ or $6$ solutions $(m,n)$ satisfying $mn(m+n)\neq0$ and $\gcd(m,n)=1$. The conjecture was checked computationally for $k\leq10^{15}$; proving it amounts to establishing uniqueness of the relevant norm representations beyond the six transformations described in the paper.
object.source_name: Patrick Morton and Serban Raianu, “Arithmetic properties of 3-cycles of quadratic maps over Q”, arXiv:2105.07435 (2022).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.07435

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of May 2021).

object.title: The polynomial zero-avoidance conjecture on the unit ball
object.statement:
Let $P_1,\ldots, P_N\in \mathbb R[x_1, \ldots, x_d]$ be polynomials, and let $\delta_1,\ldots, \delta_N>0$ satisfy

$$
\sum_{k=1}^N \delta_k\deg P_k\leq 1.
$$

**Polynomial zero-avoidance conjecture.** There exists a point $p\in B^d\subset\mathbb R^d$ such that, for every $k=1,\ldots,N$, the point $p$ is at distance at least $\delta_k$ from the zero set of $P_k$.

This conjecture simultaneously generalizes Bang's theorem and zero-avoidance results for polynomials. The supplied text gives partial results and a complex projective analogue, but does not state that the real-ball conjecture has been resolved.
object.source_name: Alexey Glazyrin, Roman Karasev and Alexandr Polyanskii, “Covering by planks and avoiding zeros of polynomials”, arXiv:2112.05382 (2022).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05382

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of December 2021).

object.title: Short-interval upper-bound conjecture for k-full numbers
object.statement:
Let $k\ge 2$ be an integer, let $x\ge 1$ be real, and let $Q_k(t)$ denote the number of $k$-full numbers at most $t$. A number is **$k$-full** if every exponent in its prime factorization is at least $k$. **Short-interval upper-bound conjecture.** There exists a constant $C_k\ge 1$ such that

$$
Q_k(x+y)-Q_k(x)\le C_k y^{1/k}
$$

uniformly for $1\le y\le x$. This would give a uniform bound for the number of $k$-full numbers in short intervals, analogous to the bound for perfect $k$-th powers; its status is not resolved in the supplied text.
object.source_name: Tsz Ho Chan, “A note on powerful numbers in short intervals”, arXiv:2207.08874 (2022).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.08874

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of July 2022).

object.title: Periodicity refinements for Romik's sequence $d(n)$ modulo powers of primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$
object.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p\equiv1\pmod4$, let $e\ge1$, and let $(d(n))_{n\ge1}$ be the sequence defined in the paper. **The fourth conjecture.** (1) The sequence $d(n)$ modulo $p^e$ is eventually periodic, with a not necessarily minimal period length

$$
\frac18p^{e-1}(p-1)^2.
$$

(2) There exists a constant $C_{p,e}$ such that

$$
d\left(n+\frac{p^{e-1}(p-1)}4\right)\equiv C_{p,e}d(n)\pmod{p^e}
$$

for all $n\ge1$, and

$$
C_{p,e}^{(p-1)/2}\equiv1\pmod{p^e}.
$$

The conjecture refines the paper's periodicity theorem. The authors note that computer data suggest pure periodicity, but deliberately conjecture only eventual periodicity; item (2) strengthens and generalises an earlier conjecture attributed to Wakhare.

object.title: The no-fragmentation criterion for plateaux in the expanded quantum infinite well
object.statement: Let $N$ be the parameter appearing in the expanded quantum infinite well, let $\Lambda\in\mathbb{Q}$, and assume that there is no fragmentation. A **plateau** is a plateau of the probability distribution studied in the paper. **No-fragmentation plateau conjecture.** There exists a plateau if and only if $2N\Lambda$ is an odd integer. Moreover, the plateau is unique. The preceding discussion says that this is suggested by computer simulations and would cover all cases in which plateaux appear for rational $\Lambda$; its status is not resolved in the supplied text.

object.title: Martínez–Roldán-Pensado–Rubin's 2-colored line-transversal conjecture
object.statement: Let $\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_1\uplus\mathcal{K}_2$ be a finite 2-colored family of convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Suppose that every $K_1\in\mathcal{K}_1$ and $K_2\in\mathcal{K}_2$ satisfy $K_1\cap K_2\neq\emptyset$. **Martínez–Roldán-Pensado–Rubin's conjecture.** There is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for some $i\in\{1,2\}$, at least $c|\mathcal{K}_i|$ members of $\mathcal{K}_i$ can be crossed by a single line. The conjecture is a strengthening of line-transversal results for pairwise intersecting convex sets in three dimensions, and the paper identifies it as an open problem.
object.source_name: Natan Rubin, “On Lines Crossing Pairwise Intersecting Convex Sets in Three Dimensions”, arXiv:2601.17913 (2026).

object.title: The power-of-two values conjecture for the Conway-type sequence d(n)
object.statement:
Let $d(n)$ be the Conway-type integer sequence, and let $I_K$ denote its generation domains, with $I_{-1}=\{1,2\}$. **Power-of-two values conjecture.** The sequence satisfies

$$
d(2^k)=0\quad\text{for }k\geq 1,
$$

and

$$
d(2^k+1)=-1\quad\text{for }k\geq 2.
$$

The claim describes two exact values at the beginning of each power-of-two scale. The source reports that it has been numerically verified to high order of $k$, but no proof or resolution is provided there.
object.source_name: Klaus Pinn, “Study of Meta-Fibonacci Integer Sequences by Continuous Self-Referential Functional Equations”, arXiv:2603.17509 (2026).

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17509

object.title: Eventual p-adic periodicity conjecture for generalized j-Euler numbers
object.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime number, let $m$ be a divisor of $p-1$ or let $m=2$, and let $q$ be the least common multiple of $2$ and $p-1$. Let $j$ be the parameter in the generalized $j$-Euler numbers $\{\mathcal{E}_n^{(d,j)}\}$, defined by

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathcal{E}_{n}^{(d,j)}\frac{t^n}{n!}=\left(1+\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{t^{dl}}{(dl+j)!}\right)^{-1}.
$$

**Eventual p-adic periodicity conjecture.** The numbers $\mathcal{E}_{mpn}^{(mp,j)}$ are $p$-adic integers, and for every positive integer $r$ there is a positive integer $n_0$ such that

$$
\mathcal{E}_{mpn+qp^r}^{(mp,j)}\equiv\mathcal{E}_{mpn}^{(mp,j)}\pmod{p^r}
$$

for every $n\geq n_0$.
This conjecture predicts eventual $p$-adic periodicity for a composite-parameter family of generalized Euler numbers. The paper reports computational evidence but the supplied text gives no resolution.
object.source_name: Yuta Nishibuchi, “p-adic Congruences of Generalized Euler Numbers and Relations to Even Zeta Values”, arXiv:2605.10677 (2026).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10677

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of May 2026).

object.title: The stronger second-largest-value conjecture for quadratic exponential sums
object.statement:
Let $m\geq 3$ be odd, let $n$ be a non-negative integer, and let $f$ be a quadratic polynomial in $n$ variables modulo $m$. Write $q=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2m}\right)$ and let $S(f,n,m)$ denote the associated normalized quadratic exponential sum. **Stronger form of the conjecture.**

$$
\left|S(f,n,m)\right|\leq\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^{\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor}.
$$

Moreover, if

$$
\left|S(f,n,m)\right|<\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^{\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor},
$$

then

$$
\left|S(f,n,m)\right|\leq\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^{\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor+1}.
$$

This refines the proposed global bound by controlling the next possible magnitude of a quadratic exponential sum. The paper states that the global conjecture has been verified for quadratic $f$ when $n\leq 10$, but the stronger assertion remains open.
object.source_name: Eduardo Duenez, Steven J. Miller, Howard Straubing and Amitabha Roy, “Incomplete Quadratic Exponential Sums in Several Variables”, arXiv:math/0412063 (2005).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0412063

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of December 2004).

object.title: Hoffman's conjecture for symmetric triple series
object.statement:
Let $A=3$ and let $n\geq 0$ be an integer. Define

$$
K_1=k_1+\frac{5n}{2}+2,\qquad K_2=k_2+\frac{3n}{2}+1,\qquad K_3=k_3+\frac{n}{2}.
$$

For a polynomial $P(K_1,K_2,K_3)$ in any of the four families specified in Theorem 
$$
of the source, with the stated parity conditions on its non-negative exponents, consider the series
$$

\sum_{k_1\geq k_2\geq k_3\geq 1}\frac{P(K_1,K_2,K_3)}{(k_1+2n+2)_{n+1}^{A}(k_2+n+1)_{n+1}^{A}(k_3)_{n+1}^{A}}.

$$
**Hoffman's symmetric-series conjecture.** Whenever this series is convergent, Theorem
$$
 holds: it is a rational linear combination of multiple zeta values of depth at most $3$, with neither $\zeta(2,2)$ nor $\zeta(2,2,2)$ appearing; and, if the additional condition $(8)$ holds, it is a rational linear combination of the explicitly listed values $1$, $\zeta(2)$, $\zeta(3)$, $\zeta(2,3)$, $\zeta(3,2)$, $\zeta(3,3)$, $\zeta(2,2,3)$, $\zeta(2,3,2)$, $\zeta(2,3,3)$, $\zeta(3,2,2)$, $\zeta(3,2,3)$, $\zeta(3,3,2)$, and $\zeta(3,3,3)$. The source says this was checked computationally for $n\leq 2$ and leaves the general case open; in particular, the open problem is to prove that $\zeta(2,2)$ does not appear.
object.source_name: Stéphane Fischler, “Multiple series connected to Hoffman's conjecture on multiple zeta values”, arXiv:math/0609799 (2007).
object.references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609799

Status: **open** according to the source (as of September 2006). “Since Theorem does not say more than Theorem about the depth 1 part, the open problem in Conjecture is to prove that $\zeta(2,2)$ does not appear.”
